Thank you very much, Your Excellency, Madam Maria Teresa Lazaro, Secretary of Foreign Affairs of the Philippines, Senator the Honorable Penny Wong, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Australia, Your Excellency, Madame Ana Claudia Roschbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat, Excellencies, distinguished participants, well, good afternoon and a very warm welcome. I would like, first of all, to express my sincere appreciation to UNDRR, Philippines and Japan, our co-organizers, as well as to our ASEAN colleagues, ASEAN partners, and United Nations representatives for joining us today. Now, as we approach the final milestone of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the risk landscape is becoming increasingly complex. Climate change is intensifying the frequency and impacts of disasters, while demographic, technological, and socioeconomic changes are creating new and interconnected risks. ASEAN remains among the most disaster-prone regions in the world. Disaster takes lives, damage livelihoods and infrastructure, disrupt essential services, and can reverse hard-won development gains. This reminds us that resilience is not only a disaster management issue, it is a development imperative. We must move beyond responding after disasters occur towards anticipating risks, reducing vulnerabilities, and acting before disasters strike. ASEAN has a strong foundation for this regional approach. First, we have the ASEAN Agreement on Disaster Management, Emergency Response and its work programme 2026-2030. Second, the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 and the Complementarities Initiative 2.0. And third, the Asian UN Joint Strategic Plan of Action on Disaster Management 2026-2030. These frameworks provide an important basis for linking disaster risk reduction, climate action, and sustainable development. Now looking towards 2030 and beyond, the Sendai Framework, I would like to highlight three priorities that we would like to see ASEAN advance together. First, better data, timely, comprehensive and precise data are essential to ensure that policies, preparedness and emergency response reflect the needs of different groups. We must strengthen our capacity to collect share and use such data effectively with continued technical support and knowledge transfer from our partners. Second, timely and trusted information. In crisis, information can spread as quickly as the disaster itself. Misinformation can undermine public confidence and complicate response efforts. We therefore need proactive, coordinated crisis communication supported by reliable information and rigorous fact checking. And third, rapid and coordinated action. Strong preparedness requires clear mechanism, defined responsibility, and effective communication across institutions. Standardized procedures and response protocols are particularly important when disasters are high impact and communities expect immediate coordinated assistance. Thailand certainly looks forward to working with partners to carry this agenda forward. We will host the United Nations Conference on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disaster in Bangkok in January 2027. This demonstrates our commitment to strengthening the protection of people affected by disasters while promoting a more inclusive approach to disaster response. Building on this momentum, as Thailand takes on the ASEAN chairmanship in 2028, we will further advance regional cooperation towards a stronger, safer, and more resilient ASEAN. Guided by the spirit of One ASEAN, One Response, we can strengthen our collective capacity to anticipate risks, act early, and ensure that resilience translates into practical protection for our people and communities. As ASEAN Coordinator for Sustainable Development Cooperation, Thailand looks forward to continuing this work with all of you towards 2030 and beyond. Thank you.

She is facing the risk of aging, the risk of gender, the risk about poverty, and even the geography combined. So we call this intersectional vulnerability. It's not a silo of vulnerability anymore. We have to look at different dimension of vulnerability, and this our data, this kind of thing is not in our data. The data is not seeing her yet. So who knows that she needs help when disaster happens? Good news is ASEAN already has planned. We have ADMIR work program. We have ASEAN declaration for people with disability. We have PGI that you already mentioned. This principle of PGI said that we have to care for people with disability, women, older people, older person and children, they all must be protected. They must lead and they also have to participate meaningfully in decision making. But think again back to that older lady with the husband. She is exactly the kind of leader that this framework envisions. But today, she is still invisible by the data and she is still unsupported by the system. So the challenge is very clear. We have to translate the ASEAN commitment into action, especially at the village level, where disability, vulnerability, and gender and disaster risk and even climate change live together every day. And we are going to see the pattern of aging people because ASEAN is aging. So in Thailand, we try to answer this question through practice. So let me introduce some of the example of the field work that we have been working since the Sendai Framework. First, we co-design with people with disability. You may have heard before that we have to consult persons with disability when we do things, we plan the programme. But we don't consult anymore. We decide with them. We work with them from the very beginning. So when we wrote the Thailand First Manual on Inclusive Shelter Management, we did not write it from Bangkok. We work together with the person with disability and community leaders, boys and girls, and they are the ones who tell us what kind of accessible shelter Lily needs. It's not the roof first and ramp later on. We start from the very beginning together. And second, what we did was we rehearsed, we did not just do the planning, we rehearsed and practised. With UNDP Thailand, we ran evacuation drill in school in tsunami area. And we make sure that students with disability, teacher with disability, and even school personnel with disability will participate in the drill. The plan on paper is not enough. We must practice with real people until safety become muscle memory. And third, we scale up. We move national policy into field practice. We have JC capacity building with government officer, we have Jesse capacity building with rescuers so that when they plan their things, they can have Jesse lens to look at their activities. Let me show you this real drill. It's not post AI photo. It's the photo of the field that I really love to go into. I love to work in the field with people. So, you see the the the photo in the middle, the sign language interpreter, she stand with the DTPM officer. This is a training for deaf people. We know that the warning that shout will never reach people who cannot hear. So I have to train sign language interpreter on the evacuation drill, early warning protocol, so that when there's something happen, they, the sign language interpreter, can connect the dots with person with disability, especially the deaf. And then do you see the map? They are all deaf people drawing the map. That is part of community-based disaster risk reduction, especially for the deaf people, because they say that if we have training, especially for the deaf, It's better for them to exchange the idea and understand the context and be able to solve their own problem because they have their own culture and their own belief and their own limitation. So they were able to complete CBDRM planning, to my surprise as well. But after the training, they were so strong in communication, in understanding the context of disaster management. And you see the photograph of the student touching the fire extinguisher, those are the blind student. And that moment, it sparked not only curiosity, it sparked the courage to be self-resilient too. And the next two photograph of the rescue, we have people with disability participating in the evacuation drill of the military and the government. And We know that lifting the person with disability to safety takes training, it's not just speed. Move faster will not move you anywhere if you have no one to train how to move you. So this is how inclusion looks like in reality in the field. It's not the policy on paper, it's where people work together before the next disaster comes. So my request to this room is very simple. As ASEAN renew the frameworks, let disability be part of the what we measure, not just what we say. And mandates must move beyond aspiration. We must include disability disaggregated target and funded reporting so that we can see who is at risk and who is being reached. And as the new global disaster treaty advance, Please keep persons with disabilities at the table, not just as a token group, but as leaders who can shape the standard in line with CRPD. So I believe that disability-inclusive disaster risk reduction has been practiced across ASEAN countries already, and we already share what we learn from each other because I also work in ASEAN countries as well. So I would like to call on the government to provide the opportunity, we need opportunity and resources to bring forward what already work in the community, share it, learn from it and scale it across the region, because resilience cannot be built in isolation. We need people to work together, we need people from disability sector to work with disaster management sector so that they can understand each other. And Thailand experience is not a finished business. It's just a test model. And we think that we can share with other countries. And we think that we should work together to make resilient, the real resilient. Okay, that's, thank you, that's from me.

Thank you, Dr. Barichard. So now I'd like to invite Dr. Jeff Schlegelmilch, Faculty Director, National Center for Disaster Preparedness from Columbia Climate School, a perspective from the academia. You have the floor, sir.

Wonderful, thank you. Thank you so much. And in fact, it's the least predictive part on how a disaster plays out. At Columbia, we built this climate finance vulnerability index looking at concessional finance and trying to understand who had the most climate risk while also looking at vulnerability and capacity to cope. But also, what was the ability to access finance and financial instruments to help cover that? And one thing we found was virtually no correlation between hazard exposure. And the ASEAN region is a part of that story, where we actually found one country that was in the top 10 of the most ready to respond, despite being among the most hazard-prone. And that's not an accident. right? Because it's not just about the hazard, it's what do we do about it. You've heard about many, many great things that have been done in the presentations before mine. I'll note the ASEAN Agreement on Disaster Management and Emergency Response was the world's first legally binding regional disaster instrument in 2005. The ASEAN Coordinating Center for Humanitarian Assistance in 2011 is a model for global collaboration and regional partnership. The CDREF and AGCF disaster insurance facility and green insurance finance facility, respectively, were launched in 2019, leading the way for how we pay for and underwrite resilience. The 2022 Anticipatory Action Framework commits member states to acting on forecast before impact, which we know consistently saves. And just this year, the CDRF and AHA center agreement, really creating direct financial triggers to disaster, to the release of funds, are again, sort of showing leadership in this space. So I would really sort of play up kind of three priorities. One of them is, you know, the vast majority of spending on disasters is reactive. after the fact. And we know, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, it's far more effective in saving lives, livelihoods, and economies to spend it ahead of time. A few examples from the region in Vietnam, $1.1 million in mangrove restoration saves about $7.3 million annually in sea **** maintenance. There are estimates that effective early warning systems in Southeast Asia alone could avert $8.7 to $13.1 billion a year. So we should do this, and we should keep doing this, and we should build off of things like the CDRIF program. The Philippines is building a parametric program, one that pays on a measured trigger, which we've seen to be very effective in disasters. There are many, many successes, and of course, I'm just highlighting just a few. The other, I would say, is that somewhere is to treat social capital as infrastructure. Somewhere between Hyogo and Sendai, the role of social capital was diminished in favor of scaling the administrative planning and technical advancements in early warning systems. I'm not saying it's the wrong call, but what I am saying is that in the research that's been done since, we found social capital, and by that I mean the everyday networks of trust and relationship between neighbors, has emerged as one of the strongest predictors and facilitators of response and recovery. It's one of the best investments that we can make that has really grown in the disaster literature. And the third priority, I would say, is own the evidence base. There is a unfortunate reality. Disaster research output right now is concentrated in the United States, Europe, and increasingly China. It's not a capability gap and we are seeing a lot of ground being made. The successor to Sendai will similarly be influenced by evidence that is visible. And so keep building that evidence base. Okay. Sometimes I wrote this section and I put my head down. I'm going to get in trouble. Okay. So the sometimes being a non politically aligned academic, I have this wonderful thing called academic freedom. And sometimes with that comes the burden of saying the uncomfortable thing. We all know disasters are getting worse.
